examples.text: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web (WWW)!
The Fujita scale was created by Ted Fujita (Tetsuya Fujita) in 1971!

To learn about a scientist and an invention, read a reliable biography, museum article, or science book. Record the scientist’s name, the invention, and the source. Compare sources when their accounts differ; a famous discovery is not always an invention.
Vehicles like jeepneys use springs to soak up the jolt and keep the ride smooth over bumps!
Many phones today have a digital compass that uses Earth's magnetic field for maps! So handy!
A dam's lake does more than make electricity! It stores drinking water, helps farms grow food, and stops downstream floods.
Filipino farmers use pheromone traps — lures with artificial sex scents — to catch male pest insects and keep their numbers down.
Fuel is anything that can burn, like wood, paper, or gasoline!
When wood is fully burned, ash is left behind and smoke rises into the air!
Iron turns into flaky rust when it reacts with both oxygen and water!
Meet the noble gases in our air: argon, neon, and helium! They are super chill and hardly react.

How long does a plastic water bottle take to decompose?

Up to 450 years to fully decompose in a landfill!
Since ancient times, gold has been used to make beautiful jewelry, rings, and coins because it never decays!
When wood is fully burned, ash is left behind and smoke rises into the air!
Burning is a chemical change! Wood turns into ash and gases, and you can never turn it back into wood again.
When wood is fully burned, ash is left behind and smoke rises into the air!
When paper burns, it turns into ash and smoke. It can never become paper again!

Why should you never burn plastic trash?

Burning plastic releases toxic chemical gases into the air, so you should never burn trash in an open fire!

Why shouldn't we burn our trash?

Burning trash, especially plastic, releases poisonous smoke bad for our health! It's better to sort, recycle, or compost it instead.
Never mix liquid bleach with ammonia-based cleaners! It creates a toxic chloramine gas, which is very dangerous.

Why should you never burn plastic trash?

Burning plastic releases toxic chemical gases into the air, so you should never burn trash in an open fire!
Using proper toilets keeps human waste from mixing into the water we drink.
Keeping your house clean and covering food and garbage is one of the best ways to keep rats away!
Almost nothing from rice goes to waste — the straw can feed animals, and the husk can become fuel or compost.
Farmers use earthworms in vermicomposting to turn food scraps and fallen leaves into rich, natural fertilizer.

With your teacher, survey a school waste problem using the same questions for each participant. Group and classify the responses, then communicate the findings to your class. Stay open-minded: listen to different opinions and change your explanation when evidence supports a better one.
Survey questionnaires can help gather information about environmental issues and concerns in a school or community.

The brain sends orders to your muscles so you can move, walk, and hold things.
Muscles wrap around your skeleton, giving your body its shape and letting it move!
The skull is the hard bone of your head, and its job is to protect your brain.
Some of your bones act like hard armor, protecting the soft organs tucked safely inside your body.
Your stomach has strong juices, or acid, that help break down all the food you eat.

What is digestion?

Digestion is breaking down food into tiny pieces so your body can absorb it!

Why does your heart beat faster in high mountains?

In high-altitude regions with low atmospheric oxygen pressure, your heart must pump faster to deliver adequate oxygen to your tissues!
Every time you breathe out, your lungs push out carbon dioxide — a waste gas your body doesn't need anymore.
Your respiratory system — nose, trachea, and lungs — works together to bring oxygen into your blood and remove carbon dioxide!
A plant's roots soak up water and nutrients from the soil so the whole plant can use them.
Many desert plants grow very long roots that dig deep into the ground to reach hidden water.

Can a stem make its own food?

Yes! Green stems can make food using sunlight too, just like leaves do.
A plant's stem is like a pipe — it carries water and nutrients from the roots all the way up to the leaves and fruit.

How can you easily see different habitats?

A diagram showing a carabao on land and a bangus in water makes their different habitats easy to see!
Terrestrial habitats are on land, aquatic habitats are in water, and aerial habitats are in the air or high places.
The whale shark is a fish that lives in the open ocean, making it an aquatic animal!

How can you easily see different habitats?

A diagram showing a carabao on land and a bangus in water makes their different habitats easy to see!
Bats fly in the air at night! This makes them aerial animals, even though they are mammals.
Aerial animals like birds, bats, and insects have wings or special body parts to stay in the air!

How can you easily see different habitats?

A diagram showing a carabao on land and a bangus in water makes their different habitats easy to see!
In a habitat diagram, the ground is at the bottom, water is a blue area, and the sky is above to place each animal properly!

Make a habitat table with plants and animals from the Philippines. Examples: garden—gumamela and butterflies; rice field—rice and frogs; seashore—beach grasses and crabs; mangrove swamp—mangrove trees and fish. Record what you actually observe; not every habitat contains every example.
A garden is a dry land habitat, while a rice field is wet! That's why they host very different plants and animals.
Frogs are common in Philippine rice fields, ponds, and streams, and children often see them during the rainy season.

A garden and rice field have fresh water, while a seashore and mangrove swamp have salty water that mixes with the tide!
Mangroves are home to many different animals, such as fish, crabs, birds, and even monkeys and snakes.

A life cycle flow chart uses arrows to show the correct order of stages, like egg to caterpillar to chrysalis to butterfly!
A butterfly begins its life as a tiny egg, usually laid by the female butterfly on a leaf.
A tadpole has a long tail for swimming, but the adult frog has no tail and uses its legs to jump!
Did you know a tadpole isn't a fish? It's actually a baby frog that will grow legs and lose its tail!
A human baby is born helpless and needs years of care, but a little chick can walk soon after hatching!
Chickens and humans have similar life cycles! We both grow gradually and do not have a metamorphosis stage.
A human baby is born helpless and needs years of care, but a little chick can walk soon after hatching!
The human life cycle has five major stages: birth, infancy, childhood, adolescence, and adulthood.
A life cycle flow chart uses arrows to show the correct order of stages, like egg to caterpillar to chrysalis to butterfly!
In a life cycle flow chart, the last arrow points back to the first stage because the adult produces eggs to start the cycle again!
Cattle are herbivores, so they eat grass and leafy plants.
A goat is a herbivore -- it eats grass, leaves, and small plants.
The crocodile is a carnivore — it eats fish, birds, and other animals!
Crocodiles are carnivores — they eat meat like fish, birds, and other animals.
Pigs are omnivores, so they eat both plants and meat.
The civet, or alamid, is an omnivore that eats fruit, insects, small animals, and eggs.
People are part of food chains too — as omnivores we eat plants like rice and vegetables and animals like fish and chicken, connecting us to the Sun through our food.

Draw this Philippine food chain: rice plant → grasshopper → frog → snake. The arrows point from the food to the eater, showing energy transfer. Label the grasshopper a herbivore and the frog and snake carnivores. This is one possible chain, not every feeding relationship.

What is an apex predator?

An apex predator is a carnivore at the very top of the food chain — an animal that almost nothing else hunts, like a lion or a shark.
People are part of food chains too — as omnivores we eat plants like rice and vegetables and animals like fish and chicken, connecting us to the Sun through our food.
Before testing, sort your objects into rigid and soft groups! Then, guess which group will change shape more easily.
To find the right force, a class pushes a rigid box harder and harder until it moves, then records that exact force!
Before testing, sort your objects into rigid and soft groups! Then, guess which group will change shape more easily.
A hand lens helps learners see tiny dents or bends that appear on a soft object after just a gentle push!
Before testing, sort your objects into rigid and soft groups! Then, guess which group will change shape more easily.
A great record for a shape-change test is a table! It needs columns for the object, shape before, force used, and shape after.
The gap between seeing lightning and hearing thunder shows the distance! Every 3 seconds equals about 1 kilometre, because sound travels about 340 metres per second.

How do we find out how fast something runs?

We use a stopwatch! It measures time in seconds to see how fast an object moves.

How do we measure how long something takes to move?

We use a stopwatch or clock to measure exactly how long it takes to move!
Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time for the whole trip!
If two things travel the exact same distance, the one that takes less time is the faster one!
On a distance-time graph, the slope shows your average speed! A steeper line means you're going faster, while a flat line means you've stopped moving.

Which axis shows time and which shows distance?

The x-axis is the horizontal line at the bottom and usually shows time. The y-axis is the vertical line going up and usually shows distance.

Draw a distance–time graph with time in seconds horizontally and distance in meters vertically. Plot (0, 0), (1, 2), (2, 4), and (3, 6). Joining these points gives a straight rising line: 2 meters each second is constant speed. Label both axes and units.

A force can speed up, slow down, or completely change the direction of a moving object!
Push a merry-go-round and watch it spin! Give it more pushes, and it spins even faster and faster!
A force can speed up, slow down, or completely change the direction of a moving object!
A force is needed to change an object's motion—to start it, stop it, or change its direction!
You need a force to start a still object moving, and another force to stop it!
A force can speed up, slow down, or completely change the direction of a moving object!

What happens when you push or pull harder?

A stronger push or pull makes an object move faster or go farther! Try kicking a ball softly, then hard.
Stretch a rubber band too far and it won't return to shape — it may snap!
A spider's dragline silk stretches a little under its weight, softening a fall without breaking.
Crushing or bending a can is a physical change! It is still metal even though its shape changed.
Solid materials can be changed by cutting, tearing, folding, twisting, bending, stretching, and pressing.
Solid materials can be changed by cutting, tearing, folding, twisting, bending, stretching, and pressing.
When you squeeze clay with your hands, the force changes its shape, making it flat or forming a new figure.

What is the first step to make sugar from sugarcane?

The sugarcane is crushed to squeeze out its sweet juice!
Every magnet has two (2) poles: a north (N) pole and a south (S) pole!
When you put two like poles together, they push apart and repel each other!
Magnets stick only to three special metals: iron, nickel, and cobalt!
Did you know a magnet attracts only a few metals, like iron, nickel, and cobalt?
Test it yourself! Touch paper clips to a magnet. The most clips stick at the ends or poles, proving the poles are the strongest parts!

What happens when you test different objects with a magnet?

Things made of iron are attracted! But plastic, rubber, and wood will not be pulled.
Magnets stick only to three special metals: iron, nickel, and cobalt!
A magnet is amazing because it can pull iron even without directly touching it!
Light doesn't need air or any material to travel through! It can zoom right across the empty vacuum of space all by itself.
Sunlight reaches Earth as an electromagnetic wave through the empty vacuum of space, meaning light does not need air to move!
Very loud sounds can damage the tiny parts inside your ear and weaken your hearing.
Super loud sounds can actually hurt your ears! That's why it's smart to stay away from noises that are too intense.
Energy is simply your ability to do work or cause a cool change to happen!
A rice cooker changes electrical energy into heat energy! It uses this heat to cook the rice.
Food gives the body the energy it needs to make heat and stay warm.
Light is a form of energy, and plants use it to make their own food!
When something burns, it gives off awesome heat and bright light!
A firefly can glow all on its own—it makes light right from inside its own body.
The maya bird makes short, repeated chirping sounds that we often hear in the morning.

How do doctors see inside the body?

They use ultrasound in hospitals to make pictures, like a baby sonogram!
When something burns, it gives off awesome heat and bright light!
In a dapog stove, burning firewood releases heat that cooks delicious food!
Sandy soil drains water super fast after rain! But clay soil holds moisture and turns into sticky mud.

Why does sandy soil dry up so fast?

Because it has larger particles! This lets water drain through it very quickly.
Sandy soil drains water super fast after rain! But clay soil holds moisture and turns into sticky mud.
In a soil test, clay-rich soil holds lots of water while sandy soil drains fast! This shows different soils keep different amounts of water for our plants.

Sand has larger mineral particles than silt, and clay has the smallest of these three. Loam combines sand, silt, and clay. These different particle mixtures help explain why soils hold and drain water differently. Compare samples rather than judging only by color.
Scientists use a soil texture triangle to name a soil by its mix of sand, silt, and clay.
Loam has both big and small pores! This means it drains well, yet still stores water for plants.

In a drainage test, sandy soil may release water in seconds, while clay takes much longer to drip.

Why are rice fields flooded with water?

The rice plant likes very wet soil.
Like other plants, a citrus tree needs water, soil, and sunlight to grow and bear fruit.
Fresh water is precious because only a small amount is available — and people, animals, and plants all need it to live!
River water is fresh, meaning it is not salty like the sea! Because of this, many animals and plants depend on rivers for clean water.
For a soil experiment, plant the exact same number of seeds at the same depth in each pot of different soil!
Use a pH strip to test the acidity of each soil type before planting, and don't forget to record the color change!
For a soil experiment, plant the exact same number of seeds at the same depth in each pot of different soil!
Use the exact same pot with the same drainage holes so water drains equally in all your setups!
In the Philippines, our temperature almost never drops to 0 degrees Celsius, making snow a super rare sight!
Did you know PAGASA measures the air temperature? They do this to help us know what the weather will be like!
A barometer measures air pressure, and it helps us forecast the weather!
Meet the barometer! This is the special instrument that measures air pressure.
A wind vane, or weather vane, is a helpful tool! It shows the direction the wind is coming from, but not its speed.

How do we measure how fast the wind is blowing?

We measure wind speed using a spinning instrument called an anemometer!
A wind vane shows which direction the wind is coming from! It spins so its pointer always faces into the wind.
A wind vane, or weather vane, is a helpful tool! It shows the direction the wind is coming from, but not its speed.
Humidity is the amount of water vapor in the air, and we measure it using a hygrometer!
When a hygrometer shows high humidity, the air is full of moisture and feels sticky and muggy — yuck!
Catch the rain! A rain gauge is the instrument that measures the rainfall.
Nimbostratus clouds are dark and thick! They bring steady rain that can last for several hours.
Nimbostratus clouds are dark and thick! They bring steady rain that can last for several hours.
High, thin cirrus clouds mean fair weather, while low, gray stratus clouds can bring drizzle or rain!
A thermometer measures temperature — it tells you how hot or cold the air, water, or your body is!
A digital thermometer is super easy to read! It shows the exact temperature as clear numbers on a small screen.
A barometer measures air pressure, and it helps us forecast the weather!
Meet the barometer! This cool tool is used to measure air pressure, also known as atmospheric pressure.
An anemometer has three or four small cups that turn in the wind — the faster they spin, the stronger the wind!

How do we measure how fast the wind is blowing?

We measure wind speed using a spinning instrument called an anemometer!
A wind vane spins to show where the wind comes from! If it blows from the north, we call it a north wind.
A wind vane shows which direction the wind is coming from! It spins so its pointer always faces into the wind.
Humidity is the amount of water vapor in the air, and we measure it using a hygrometer!
A digital hygrometer uses electronic sensors to measure exactly how much water vapor is floating in the air!
Catch the rain! A rain gauge is the instrument that measures the rainfall.
Place your rain gauge in an open area away from trees and buildings. They can block the rain and make the reading wrong!
When we record weather instrument readings every day, we can spot cool patterns, like exactly when the rainy or dry season arrives!
A sunshine recorder (Campbell-Stokes recorder) uses a glass sphere to focus sunlight onto a card that records hours of bright sunshine each day!
A weather chart tracks if it's sunny, rainy, or cloudy every day, helping us spot patterns in the weather!
Wearing boots or shoes without holes helps keep flood water from touching your skin.
Caught outside with no shelter? Crouch down low and make yourself as small as you can!
The Sun makes its energy through nuclear fusion! It joins hydrogen together to form helium.

What is the Sun mostly made of?

The Sun is mostly made of hydrogen, along with some helium!
Wow, the Sun is huge! About 1.3 million Earths could fit right inside it!
About 1.3 million Earths could fit inside the Sun! That is a giant space!
Solar energy comes directly from the bright light and cozy heat of our sun!
The Sun is the main natural source of heat and light energy for the Philippines and our whole Earth!
Plant a stick in the ground for a sundial! As the Sun moves across the sky, the stick's shadow shifts and changes length, showing time passing.

Can you build your own sun-clock?

Yes! Just stick an upright stick in the ground. Mark where the shadow tip lands each hour to make your own sundial!
In the Philippines, your shadow is shortest around noon because the sun is almost directly overhead!
Your shadow is longest in the early morning because the low angle of the Sun blocks light across a greater distance!
In the morning, the shadow points west because the sun is in the east; a shadow always points away from the light.
In the morning, the shadow points west because the Sun is in the east. As the Sun moves west, the shadow slowly swings toward the east!

With your teacher, keep a shadow stick fixed in one place. At different times, mark its shadow’s tip and record the length and direction. Earth’s rotation makes the Sun appear to change position, so the shadow changes too. Observe the shadow, never look directly at the Sun.
The sun is the original source of energy for almost every food chain on Earth!
Many reef builders live with tiny algae that need sunlit water! This means some underwater life depends on sunlight reaching the shallows.

How do we know our Sun guesses are right?

After class, check a trustworthy book or science site! This confirms our ideas about sunshine instead of just voting on them.

Where can we check facts about sunlight and weather?

A PAGASA or NASA education page is a trustworthy secondary source! You can use it to confirm class ideas about sunlight and weather.
